title: Taking a look at Set a Watch: Swords of the Coin
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VLJJ9zvdj2Y

Daniel (@dungeondive) takes a look at *Set a Watch: Swords of the Coin*, the standalone follow-up to *Set a Watch*, and warns up front that his thoughts are scattershot, because the game is overflowing with them. Four heroes (he fields Heretic, Artificer, Bounty Hunter and Barbarian) escort a caravan across eight nights, each night ambushed by a battle line of monsters. Lose every power on the heroes standing watch and the game is lost.

Each hero rolls a distinct die type, then one hero tends camp for the night: feeding the bonfire, whose level dictates how many monsters in the line you can see and attack; chopping wood, scouting the monster deck, healing exhausted power cards, or swapping in a kinder respite map card. Every hero must camp twice over the trek. Daniel's Bounty Hunter had a bad night and the fire dropped below two, leaving his watch fighting shapes in the dark. Unhallowed mini-bosses such as the Prince of Vultures and the Clockwork Commander get shuffled in as things worsen.

His one struggle is information load: four heroes with five unique powers apiece is twenty things worth using. Yet he would not want fewer, because the game makes him feel like a cohesive unit struggling to survive. He compares it to *Ghost Stories* without the snowballing cruelty, a tower defence with a single tower, packed into a box that doubles as the play area.

----

Twenty powers across four heroes: rich, or too much for solo? Where is your limit for running a whole party alone?
